Agrippina the Younger. A prominent Roman noblewoman and empress of the first century CE, infamous for her political ambition and ruthlessness in advancing her son's power. Born around fifteen CE into one of Rome's most prominent families, she maneuvered her way to supreme influence as the wife of Claudius and mother of Nero.

Agrippina was the granddaughter of Emperor Augustus and sister of the mad Emperor Caligula, so she came from one of Rome's most powerful dynasties. Around forty-nine CE, she married her uncle Claudius—her mother's brother—in what was a politically ambitious marriage that made her empress. She allegedly poisoned Claudius with mushrooms to secure the throne for her son Nero, though accounts vary and historical certainty is elusive.

She engineered the adoption of Nero as Claudius's heir, sidelining the emperor's biological son Britannicus. She became one of the most powerful women in Roman history, with coins minted bearing her image alongside Nero's. But after Nero's accession, he grew resentful of her influence and political interference. She attempted to maintain dominance over him, but it didn't work.

Around fifty-nine CE, Nero had her murdered, allegedly after multiple assassination attempts, as he sought absolute control. Her legacy is one of palace intrigue, alleged murder, and a son who would himself become one of Rome's most reviled emperors.
